newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia's federation economy grows steadily.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia's federation economy grows steadily.

text.p: The 1997 indicators in Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation show a constantly growing economy with inflation under control, foreign analysts said on Friday.

"On the basis of January to April statistics, the (federation) economy continues to be strong and inflation well-controlled," an authoritative economic expert, who asked not to be further identified, told Reuters.
He spoke after analysing the federation's indicators.
The Statistics Bureau reported a slide in industrial output of 7.5 percent in April compared to the previous month and a rise in retail prices of 2.9 percent.
Analysts dismissed the monthly fluctuations because none of the figures were seasonably adjusted.
"Even in developed countries, month-to-month fluctuations are not terribly meaningful," the economic expert said.
Bosnia emerged from a devastating 1992-1995 war as one country but effectively divided in two entities by a peace accord -- the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic.
The federation saw a 50 percent annual growth rate in 1996 which was mainly fuelled by foreign donors' capital in the emergency repair of the country's damaged infrastructure.
Bosnian Serbs saw only two percent of an estimated $1.2 billion committed in Bosnia in 1996 and marginal growth as a result of their non-compliance with the peace accord's civilian provisions.
The World Bank said last month it expected the federation's growth to continue in 1997 but not on the same 50 percent level. The projection is a 35 percent a year growth for the next three years.
So a slowdown in the federation's industrial output was expected, the expert said.
"This is not falling output. Some deceleration is expected (in 1997) but definitely not a falling output."
Bosnia's peacetime government, comprised of former enemies, has yet to adopt a package of economic reforms proposed by the international community to create a market-oriented economy.

But political bickering has so far blocked progress on economic reforms which also include forming a joint central bank. The reforms are set as a condition for an approaching fund-raising conference in which foreign donors are expected to pledge $1.4 billion for reconstruction in 1997.
Funds which have not been disbursed from the $1.8 billion pledged in 1996 are still flowing into Bosnia and are supporting the climate of economic growth in the federation.
But the entire country needs to change its course towards a self-sustainable economy, the economic analyst said.
"If there is a continued political deadlock and lack of reform, which I don't expect, but is a possibility nevertheless, then definitely the economic programme would go off track."
The fund-raising conference has already been postponed several times because of Bosnia's lack of economic legislation.
"I hope the package of economic reforms could be wrapped up by the end of next week. I think the threat of cancelling the conference really worked," the expert said.
